_comment: English bodies for pydantic-ai (framework). Mechanism per C0-1..6. Official English quotes kept verbatim. layer_position/providers not rendered — not included.

axes.model_access:
**The most model providers connectable, with a full official catalog; switching models is one string.**

The official first selling point is model-agnostic. **Official overview, verbatim**:

**Model-agnostic**: Supports **virtually every** model and provider:
OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, Cohere, Mistral, and Perplexity;
Azure AI Foundry, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, **Ollama**, LiteLLM, Groq, OpenRouter,
Together AI, Fireworks AI, Cerebras, Hugging Face, GitHub, Heroku, Vercel, Nebius,
OVHcloud, Alibaba Cloud, and SambaNova.

The official docs add a line leaving a door for in-house models. **Official wording**:

**Official wording**: "If your favorite model or provider is not listed, you can easily implement a custom model."

The official catalog splits providers into four groups.

- **9 model developers** — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google(Gemini), DeepSeek, Mistral,
  plus Cohere / xAI / Moonshot(Kimi) / Z.AI

- **6 cloud platforms** — AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud(Vertex AI), Azure Foundry,
  Alibaba Cloud, Snowflake Cortex, Heroku

- **3 local & self-hosted** — Ollama (`ollama:`), vLLM (`vLLM:`), LiteLLM (`litellm:`)
- **8 inference platforms & gateways** — Groq, Cerebras, Hugging Face, Together, Fireworks, OpenRouter
  (six inference platforms) plus Vercel AI Gateway and Pydantic AI Gateway (two gateways)

Usage is a `<provider>:<model>` prefix string, e.g. `Agent('openai:gpt-5.2')`.
The official models/overview page gives a **provider catalog table**.
Each provider row carries its service type and selection syntax.

There are also a **fallback model** and **ModelProfile**.
The latter marks capabilities like `supports_tools`, `supports_json_schema_output`.

⚠ **One boundary the official docs draw themselves**: capabilities are **not guaranteed equivalent across providers**.

**Official wording**: "Feature support depends on the model and API you select, even when two services use the same
API format."

Full behavioral equivalence after switching providers is not guaranteed by the official docs.
The official position: the same agent is portable, but per-vendor behavioral consistency needs testing.
axes.runtime:
**A pure Python library, not a service** — after install, you decide where it runs.

Install is `uv add pydantic-ai` (or the slim variant). It **does not start a server**.
The official position is "the same agent runs everywhere". **Official README, verbatim**:

"The same agent **runs everywhere you need it**: behind a web frontend, in the
terminal, on a voice call, on a **durable background queue**, in GitHub Actions, or as a plain
object you call `run()` on."

The runtime surface is yours; the official docs give these entry points:

- embedded in a web frontend (AG-UI / Vercel AI event streams)
- the terminal (official CLI `clai`)
- on-device voice sessions
- a durable background queue (that path requires wiring an engine — see the background axis)

**Who runs the agent loop**: you.
Two optional official components — the **Pydantic AI Gateway** (self-hostable) for model routing,
and **Logfire** for observability.
Both optional; neither changes the fact that "the library is run by you".

The official docs also provide GitHub Agentic Workflows, running headless on issues / PRs.
There is also a built-in web chat entry. Both are built on the same library.
axes.local_files:
**The core agent carries no file system; the official Harness provides a complete local-file kit.**

A plain `Agent` has no workspace concept.
File capability lives in the **Pydantic AI Harness**. **Official README, verbatim** (Coding agent section):

"A complete coding agent in your terminal: **workspace-rooted
file access**, **allowlisted shell**, repo orientation, planning, and **context management** that
survives long sessions."

The implementation is a set of separable **capabilities**:

- `FileSystem('.')`
- `Shell(cwd='.')`
- `RepoContext()`
- `SubAgents(...)`
- `ClearToolResults()`
- `ToolOutputLimits()`

The official docs stress Coder merely composes them. **Official wording**:

**Official wording**: "use it whole, or use the blocks it bundles directly; the two are equivalent"

**The key boundaries are written explicitly**: file access is **workspace-rooted** (scoped to the workspace),
shell is **allowlisted** (whitelist).

There is also **Monty**, officially "a sandboxed Python interpreter that runs model-written code".
It runs code written by the model.

**Unknown: the default file-access boundary at the core-SDK level (without Harness) is not stated by the official docs**
**Verified**: overview and harness pages checked.
axes.background:
**Its hardest differentiator: the official docs list eight durable-execution engines,**
and "every model and tool call becomes its own **durable** unit".

**Official durable execution page, verbatim**:

"Pydantic AI allows you to build **durable agents** that can **preserve their progress across
transient API failures and application errors or restarts**,
and handle long-running, asynchronous, and human-in-the-loop workflows with production-grade reliability."

Mechanism, **official wording**:

"Each engine wraps **every model request and tool call as its own durable unit**"

The official README lists the engines as **Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate, AWS Lambda, Kitaru, Airflow, Absurd**,
with "the **first five co-maintained** with the vendor teams".
Third parties also have a **durable execution backend builder** to plug in their own engine.

Connection example: the `TemporalDurability()` capability + `PydanticAIWorkflow`; officially:

"a run working through a background queue **survives restarts, failures, and long waits**"

⚠ **Read the boundary out loud**: the official docs dedicate one line —

"**Durability is not storage**"

Meaning: the durable engine only guarantees one run survives crashes.
It **does not store your conversation threads** — that is a separate Persistence module.

Two more limits: `run_sync()` / `run_stream_sync()` cannot be used inside tools; use `async def`.
**Each agent can attach only one durable engine**; attaching a second throws `UserError`.
axes.tools:
**The tool surface has four layers: function tools + MCP + A2A + capability composition. MCP is a core capability.**

Function tools register with `@agent.tool`. **Official wording**:

**Official wording**: "the rest of its signature and its docstring become the tool schema, arguments are validated before your code runs"

Argument errors are fed back to the LLM for retry.

**MCP officially supports two directions** (mcp/overview page):

- ① the agent connects to an MCP server and uses its tools
- ② the agent is placed inside an MCP server

The recommended approach is the **`MCP` capability**. Officially:

"It **runs the MCP server locally by default** — keeping credentials, hooks, and tracing under your control"

and a single `native=True` flag opts into the model provider's native MCP (falling back to local when unsupported).
Low-level: `MCPToolset` (`toolsets=[...]`).
**"Local by default" matters for credential control**.

⚠ **A2A is being retired.** The official integrations/a2a page states explicitly:

- `Agent.to_a2a()` and `pydantic-ai-slim[a2a]` are "**deprecated and will be removed in 2.0**"
- `fasta2a` has moved to `datalayer/fasta2a`, with a Pydantic AI bridge

**UI/interfaces**: AG-UI, Vercel AI event streams, CLI, built-in web chat, voice.
There is also the **capabilities** composition mechanism.
And **YAML/JSON agent specs** for defining agents without code.
axes.context:
**It explicitly splits "persistence" from "durability" — the core framing of this dimension.**

**Official durable execution page, verbatim**:

"**Durability is not storage** — A durable engine keeps one run
alive across crashes and restarts. It **does not store your chat threads**: saving a conversation
and picking it up later is a different problem ... laid out in **Persistence**."

i.e. the durable engine manages run survival.
**Persistence** manages saving and resuming conversation threads — a separate module.

**Harness additionally provides context management**: the official capabilities list includes **memory**,
**context management** (compaction), **persistence**. **Official README, verbatim** says Harness:

**Official wording**: "has everything an agent needs for complex, long-running work, snapped on as capabilities"

So our "state ≠ context" is split by the official docs into three: the durable run (engine), the chat thread (Persistence), context compaction.

**Unknown: the concrete trimming strategy and thresholds of compaction — the official docs give no defaults**
**Verified**: README and durable page checked.
axes.permissions:
**Human intervention is "tool-level approval"; sandboxing sits in Harness / Monty; credentials default to local.**

**HITL tool approval** is item 8 of the official overview:

"**Human-in-the-Loop Tool Approval**: Easily lets you flag
that certain tool calls **require approval** before they can proceed, **possibly depending on tool
call arguments, conversation history, or user preferences**."

This line comes from the deferred tools page.
Its level differs from other listed objects: **it intercepts "may this tool call run",
and can decide dynamically from arguments and history.**

**guardrails** also ship with Harness (the official Harness capability list includes guardrails).

**Sandbox**: the official **Monty** is "a sandboxed Python interpreter that runs model-written code".
Harness's `Shell` is **allowlisted**; `FileSystem` is **workspace-rooted**.

**Credentials**: MCP runs locally by default; officially "keeping credentials, hooks, and tracing under your control".

**Unknown: whether the core SDK has process/network-level sandboxing and built-in auth/permission boundaries is not stated by the official docs**
**Verified**: overview, durable, and mcp pages checked.
Enterprise-grade permissions and auditing are handled on the Logfire / Gateway side.
axes.fit:
**Fits: Python teams needing type safety, and anyone turning agent runs into durable ones.**

- **Python teams** building agents with "type-safe structured output + dependency injection"
- You need agent runs to become **durable** (across restarts, long waits, HITL),
  and want to use engines you already have, like Temporal / DBOS / Prefect

- Building multi-agent systems (agent delegation / hand-off / graph)
- You need first-class MCP support and want MCP **running locally to control credentials**
- You want both a thin agent loop and the official ready-made Harness (Coder / Researcher / memory / guardrails)
- You want Pydantic validation to run end to end from the data layer to agent output

**Does not fit: non-Python stacks, minimalists, and anyone needing a core-SDK-shipped sandbox.**

- TypeScript / Node teams (look at [Mastra](./mastra.md))
- Chasing minimal dependencies, not wanting Pydantic and optional capability packages (its worldview is typed end to end)
- Wanting to avoid any commercial component entirely — Logfire and Gateway are officially recommended but **optional**;
  the official docs state OTel and self-hosting are both supported

- Needing framework-shipped process-level sandbox and network policy in the core — sandboxing sits in Harness / Monty, not the core SDK

sections.与 OpenAI Agents SDK 的对照：本站最该给读者看的一张表:
Both are "Python libraries that give you an agent loop", similar in style. The differences are concrete:

| | OpenAI Agents SDK | **Pydantic AI** |
|---|---|---|
| Type system | optional dataclass / Pydantic output | **Pydantic-native**: typed output + typed dependency injection + typed tools |
| Non-OpenAI models | litellm / any-llm adapters | **native provider catalog**: `<provider>:<model>` string switching, incl. local Ollama/vLLM |
| durable execution | no dedicated engine (DIY) | **eight official engines** (Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate/AWS Lambda/Kitaru/Airflow/Absurd) |
| Upper capabilities | primitives-only | **plus Pydantic AI Harness** (memory/guardrails/sub-agents/compaction + a ready Coder) |
| Observability | Traces report to the OpenAI backend by default | **standard OpenTelemetry**, any OTLP backend; Logfire optional |

**One-line rule**: want Python's "type safety + durable" → Pydantic AI;
want minimalism, built-in guardrails, and the OpenAI ecosystem → OpenAI Agents SDK.

**Official durable execution page, verbatim**:

> Pydantic AI allows you to build **durable agents** that can **preserve their progress across

sections.MCP：两个方向都支持，且默认本地运行以控制凭据:
The official mcp/overview page describes two directions:

- ① the agent connects to an MCP server and uses its tools
- ② the agent is placed inside an MCP server

The recommended approach is the **`MCP` capability**. Officially:

> It **runs the MCP server locally by default** — keeping credentials, hooks, and tracing
> **under your control** — and lets you opt into the model provider's **native MCP support**
> with a single `native=True` flag.

Low-level: `MCPToolset` (`toolsets=[...]`).
**"Local by default" is valuable for credential control**.
Versus **"handing credentials to the provider's native MCP"**, this is an optional trade-off.
sections.A2A：官方已开始退场，注意时点:
This must be written clearly, or it will be misjudged as a long-term built-in capability.
The official integrations/a2a page headline reads:

> **Deprecated in 1.x, removed in 2.0**

- `Agent.to_a2a()` and `pydantic-ai-slim[a2a]` are deprecated, removed in 2.0.
- `fasta2a` is now maintained by **datalayer/fasta2a**.
  Since v0.6.1 it ships a Pydantic AI bridge (`agent_to_a2a`).

So the sentence "Pydantic AI supports A2A" needs a **version timestamp** to be accurate.
sections.Harness 与 Graph 是两个独立上层:
- **Pydantic AI Harness**: officially packages memory, guardrails, sub-agents, planning,
  context management (compaction), and persistence into **capabilities**,
  and ships ready-made **Coder / Researcher** complete agents.

  The official docs also stress Coder is not a black box. **Official wording**: "use it whole, or use the blocks it bundles directly; the two are equivalent".

- **`pydantic-graph`**: the official graphs page says it **can be used independently of pydantic-ai** —
  "it has **no dependency on `pydantic-ai`** and can be considered as a pure graph-based state machine library".
  The official docs also humorously note: a graph is a nail gun, not the right tool for every job.

  Conclusion: **both are optional layers grown off the core library** — which is why we still file this under coding-base.

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/framework/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/framework/_protocol.md).

**Suggested runs** (tailored to coding-base + type-safety / durable dimensions):

| # | What to test | Why it is worth testing |
|:--:|---|---|
| 1 | How many files and lines for a minimal hello agent | quantifies the real onboarding cost of the "thin agent loop" |
| 2 | Give it a Pydantic output model; verify the run must return that type | the official selling point is typed end to end — verify "the returned value is the type" |
| 3 | Run an agent with tools and structured output on an Ollama local model | the official catalog lists Ollama separately — verify real feasibility |
| 4 | Run a long task with TemporalDurability, kill the process, then resume | the core of the official durable promise — must verify |
| 5 | Code-volume comparison of agent delegation / hand-off / graph for multi-agent | the official docs give five complexity tiers — verify the selection advice |
| 6 | Credential and behavior differences: MCP capability local-by-default vs `native=True` | the official docs stress local-by-default keeps credentials under control — worth verifying |

- The default file-access boundary of the core SDK without Harness (not stated officially; overview and harness pages checked)
- Whether the core SDK has process/network-level sandboxing and built-in permission boundaries (not stated officially; sandboxing sits in Harness / Monty)
- The default trimming strategy and thresholds of Harness compaction (not stated officially)
- Billing details of the Pydantic AI Gateway (not itemized on the official pricing page; rates not recorded per D9)
- Feature alignment across the eight durable engines (not stated officially)
- Full behavioral equivalence across providers (the official docs already state it "depends on the model and API you select")
- The official 2.0 replacement path after A2A removal (the official docs point to datalayer/fasta2a)
related: **The pair most worth contrasting on our site**: both are thin Python agent-loop libraries; Pydantic AI's differentiators are Pydantic-native type safety + eight official durable-execution engines.
The counterpart in another language: TypeScript's batteries-included full-stack framework vs Python's type-safe agent loop — their answers to the "first decision point" differ.

Orchestration-layer contrast: LangGraph persists every superstep and modifies state via HITL; Pydantic AI's `pydantic-graph` is a typed state machine, and durable execution is delegated to external engines.
The official multi-agent page lists Deep Agents as the fifth (most autonomous) multi-agent form; Pydantic AI also has its own Harness — both sit on the "autonomy + files + subagents" side.
